title: Disaster for island country but games of big power: a home for displaced people and their culture

context_sources.name: Cai Rongshuo and Tan Hongjian, sea level rise and low islands, 2020
World Bank, population on land below five meters
Steven Brams, Game Theory and Politics, 2011
Duncan Snidal, The game theory of international politics, 1985

limitations: Watermark glyphs split equations and merge into words on most pages.
Table 4 leaves several country names and year cells blank or misaligned.
The Lyapunov derivative steps are partly unreadable.
Figure 6 captions swap situation 1 and situation 2.

tasks: Date the submergence of coastal states under two rise regimes
Rank states by responsibility and capacity
Assign each sinking people to a receiving state by simulated bargaining
Find the marriage and inheritance rates that keep a culture alive
Stage the policies so protection does not provoke backlash

section_map.summary: Cone model, responsibility index, pressure game, culture equation, combined policy.
Land loss creates both displaced people and a culture risk, so policy is itself a problem.
Linear density, whole-population moves, costly acceptance, pressure, shared citizenship.
Cone geography, corrected density, two rise regimes, eleven-country timetable.
Responsibility ranking, legal position, eight-player pressure game, five-country schedule.
Three-group dynamics, Lyapunov stability, staged policy.
Answers to all five problem questions in one place.
Cone robust early; ranking stable; culture sensitive to intermarriage near zero.
Sea level, refugee law, and game theory of politics.

contributions.summary: A cone plus a linear density corrected by five-meter population data, with four action-tied thresholds.
Pressure as a signed cube of the gap between private expectation and reality, so states can be pushed to do less.
An explicit stability region in the two policy levers, intermarriage and inheritance.

dependency_graph.handoff: The dated list of sinking states is what the game then assigns, one run per state
The eight highest-ranked states become the players, in rank order
The receiving state is the host population inside which the culture model then runs

assumptions.summary: Density falls linearly because high ground supports neither farming nor fishing.
Acceptance is costly in money and in local resentment, so states avoid it.
Arrivals take the new citizenship and the same rights.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: World Bank counts of people below five meters correct the density slope.
Rise rates of 2.72 mm a year in 2002 and 3.83 in 2014 fix the acceleration.

models.summary: Circular-cone geography with linear, data-corrected population density.
Eight-player pressure game with a cubic gap and a stopping rule.
Nonlinear bearer dynamics with a proved stable region.

verification.summary: Varying the index weights barely changes the ranking of the strongest states.
Bearer totals respond strongly to intermarriage only when it is near zero.

results_trace.summary: By 2050, 0.16 m and about 26.6 million people affected under acceleration.
Australia takes Tuvalu in 2030, the United States the Maldives in 2041, Canada Tonga in 2042, China the Marshall Islands in 2054, Russia Samoa.
Culture persists when intermarriage is small and inheritance is large.

writing_logic.summary: The worse scenario is shown and then withdrawn as unrealistic, so the milder one carries the claim.
A real refugee crisis is used to reject optimization in favor of a game.
Both single policies are shown to fail, which forces the staged combination.

language_observations.summary: An unpredictable disaster replaced by a headcount, and the replacement called a gain in definiteness.
Benefit and harm split across rich states and islands in one sentence, then turned into an inequality.
A row of pressure numbers narrated as what one state tells the world.
A theorem's conclusion restated as the fate of a culture, balance or disappearance.

visualization_observations.summary: Figure 1: a circular cone standing in for a country's terrain.
Figure 2: population piled on the lower part of the cone.
Figure 3: rising water cutting into the cone.
Figure 4: the eleven states at risk marked on a world map.
Figure 5: the loop of the pressure game.
Figure 6: two bearer trajectories over 700 years, captions swapped.
Figure 7: the responsibility index against two weights.
Figures 8 and 9: bearer paths as intermarriage and inheritance vary.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: Tying each percentage to a specific action makes the timetable usable rather than decorative.
Allowing negative pressure, so a state can be pushed to do less, keeps the game from being a monotone blame model.
Stating that no single policy works, and pricing each one, reads as judgment rather than advocacy.

weaknesses.summary: The game assigns five sinking states while the cone model found eleven.
The expectations and the relationship matrix, which decide the result, are never published.
The authors cannot say how far any policy moves the two culture parameters.

independent_extensions.summary: Run the game for the six sinking states left out of the timetable.
Publish the expectation vectors and the relationship matrix.
Estimate how much each policy shifts intermarriage and inheritance.

candidate_rule_impacts.summary: Split help into receiving and paying, and let capacity decide who can do the first.
Sequence policies so the one that would provoke backlash comes only after the groups get along.

unresolved_questions.question: Who receives Palau, Kiribati, Micronesia, Fiji, the Bahamas and Gambia?
What expectation vector and relationship matrix produced the timetable?
By how much does each policy move intermarriage and inheritance?
